To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mentalizing network is less activated in the autism group than in the normal group while watching animations that elicit mentalizing.

(a) people with autism have a specific difficulty in attributing mental states to other people (mentalizing); (b) mentalizing is associated with increased activity in a network of brain areas that includes the superior temporal sulci at the temporo- parietal junction and the medial prefrontal cortex; (c) people with autism show reduced functional connectivity in the brain between these areas, and between the temporo-par-ietal junction and extrastriate visual areas.

the autism group showed reduced activity in a network of brain regions associated with mentalizing (medial pre-frontal cortex, superior temporoparietal and temporal poles) and reduced functional connectivity between the superior temporoparietaal junction and extrastriate visual cortex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural basis of the attribution of mental processes to others.
understanding the neural mechanisms underlying the ability to attribute mental states to others.
the question of whether and, if so, how the brain of an individual with an autism spectrum disorder differs from that of a normal person.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mentalizing in autism is a functionally impaired, but structurally normal phenomenon.
the autistic brain does not have the ability to attribute mental states to animated figures.

there is an impairment in mentalizing, which is not a result of an inability to understand the movements of the animated shapes but is due to a failure of higher order perceptual processes to interact with the perception of biological motion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the mentalizing network is not fully functional in the autism group, but the extrastriate system that processes biological motion is fully functioning, and is the bottleneck in the mentalizing network.
the mentalizing network is less active in autism, but that the extrastriate system is equally active in both groups.

autism is characterized by a deficit in the attribution of mentalizing states, which may have its origin in a deficit in the integration of lower order perceptual information with higher order perceptual information, and in a deficit in top-down modulation of perceptual processing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are specific brain regions and circuits that support the ability to attribute mental states to others, and that these are disrupted in autism.
the mentalizing network is dysfunctional in autism.
the brain of the autistic person has a deficit in the mentalizing network that includes the medial prefrontal cortex.
